
> Same coefficients as Table 3.3, plotted with CIs across the three specifications side by side. Facility- and LGA-level heterogeneity checks (not shown as a separate numbered table) found isolated significant effects at only one or two individual sites out of roughly twenty tested, consistent with noise rather than a systematic effect.

### iii. Negative binomial comparison

A negative binomial specification, the theoretically preferred alternative given the overdispersion confirmed above, was tested against all three weather variables as a further robustness check. Across precipitation, heat, and vegetation, the negative binomial specification agrees with the primary log-transformed OLS specification in direction and in the absence of significance. Log-transformed OLS is retained as the primary specification throughout this thesis for the reasons of consistency and interpretability set out in Section II.D, not because it performs better against this alternative.

**Table 3.4.  Weather model — negative binomial comparison**

```{r tab-3-10}
render_simple_table(show_tab("tab_3_10"))
```

> Log-OLS and negative binomial coefficients side by side for all three weather variables. Both specifications agree on direction and non-significance throughout; the precipitation variable is the closest either comes to a conventional threshold, and even there both specifications remain nominally within the nulled interpretation given in Section III.C.ii.

# IV. Discussion and Synthesis

## A. What the data can show: reading the zero-dose and recovery findings together

Distance predicts ZD status once the strict definition is applied, an 87 per cent increase in the odds of zero-dose status per additional kilometre, and shows almost nothing under the primary definition, a non-significant 4 per cent increase per kilometre. Distance predicts almost nothing about recovery: once a child is flagged and a tracing attempt begins, the same variable shows no detectable effect at all, consistent with the explanation offered in Section II.C.i, that recovery here runs through SMS and phone contact rather than physical travel.

**Table 4.1.  Quantitative findings paired with field observation**

```{r tab-4-1}
render_simple_table(show_tab("tab_4_1"), widths_em = c("28em", "24em"))
```

> Three rows (distance, timing, recordkeeping) plus weather, each pairing a quantitative finding with a corroborating or complicating field observation. Field observation is contextual grounding from conversations with DATHARM staff and two PHC visits, not a structured qualitative method.

This split says something useful about DATHARM's two stated problems: finding zero-dose children, and getting them vaccinated once found. They are not the same problem, and they do not respond to the same fix. Physical reach, more outreach points, shorter travel distances, matters for the first. The second seems to depend far more on contact method and speed than on geography, an asymmetry sharpened rather than blurred by the strict-versus-primary ZD definition split: distance only shows its full strength once "zero-dose" means genuinely no contact at all, which is exactly the population for whom physical reach, not follow-up, is the binding constraint.

DATHARM's Kano coordinator estimated that roughly one in five households are missed during enumeration rounds. There is no way to check this against MCHTrack's own records, since nothing in the system tracks a household that was never reached in the first place, but it points the same way as the regression does. Every ZD count in this thesis describes children the programme managed to find, not children who exist. Distance almost certainly shapes who gets found at all, in ways this analysis, built entirely from children eventually enumerated, has no way to observe directly.

Field conversation with DATHARM's Kano coordinator adds a further layer here, describing a real state-level reversal in which method effectiveness runs the opposite way in Kano relative to Katsina: home visits reported as the more effective method in Kano specifically, against SMS in Katsina. Card verification remains the stated protocol for confirming any outcome regardless of which method makes first contact, and this thesis's pooled estimate, built to hold across both states at once, cannot on its own confirm the size of that reversal; had the analysis pooled both states from the outset without checking for it, a state-level pattern like this one could have gone unnoticed entirely.

The strict-versus-permissive recovery gap belongs in the same discussion. Recovery measured strictly, a confirmed in-network vaccination, stands at 42.6 per cent pooled across both states. Measured permissively, counting unverified off-network care, it rises to 77.2 per cent. This gap is not noise. It follows directly from the protocol described in Section II.A, which allows a tracing case to close on the strength of a card check, with no record kept of what the card actually showed. Whichever figure DATHARM reports, the distance between the two is a fact about the limits of the underlying records, and no amount of further modelling will close it. Taken together, these three findings suggest the same caution applies throughout this thesis's first two models: each coefficient is real, but each also marks the edge of what MCHTrack's records can confirm on their own.

## B. Why the weather model came back null: reading it against Sindh and Miami

The same test has been run twice elsewhere, and both times it found something. Siddiqi et al. (2025) linked daily heat data to a real-time immunisation registry in Sindh, Pakistan, and found that heat wave days significantly reduced immunisation delivery, with outreach activities hit harder than fixed-site delivery. Samano et al. (2021) linked daily heat and precipitation to an HIV clinic registry in Miami, and found both variables significantly increased missed appointments there. Neither registry carries the enumeration or verification gaps documented in Section II.A, a comparability caveat worth holding through everything that follows: these two comparator registries are themselves unlikely to be entirely clean, but they are cleaner than MCHTrack on the specific dimensions this thesis can check.

**Table 4.2.  This thesis against the two closest registry-based precedents**

```{r tab-4-2}
render_simple_table(show_tab("tab_4_2"), widths_em = c("14em", "18em", "12em", "20em"))
```

> Side-by-side comparison of outcome measured, weather exposure used, direction and significance of effect, and data-quality caveats across this thesis, Siddiqi et al. (2025) and Samano et al. (2021). Included mainly to make explicit that this thesis's null sits against two comparators that both found significant effects.

Five explanations are worth weighing. They are not mutually exclusive, and several likely operate together.

The first concerns what dominates the social calendar. Zero-visit days in this dataset cluster around specific weekdays and known religious holidays rather than spreading evenly across the year, as Section III.C.i showed. If social and operational rhythm already explains most of the swing in daily visits, little room is left for weather to explain anything further, whether or not a real weather effect exists underneath it. This matches what was heard directly in the field: across conversations with DATHARM staff and visits to two primary healthcare centres near Abuja, nobody named weather as a reason families miss appointments, even when discussion turned directly to barriers and attendance. The barriers named instead were almost entirely social, gendered, and economic. Caregiver focus group discussions conducted in Kano and Lagos found that gender-skewed household decision-making, misconceptions about immunisation, and competing socio-economic priorities were the barriers most consistently raised (Bolarinwa et al., 2025), and a companion study across six northern Nigerian states identified poor health worker attitude, ineffective documentation of immunisation appointments, and vaccine supply shortages as dominant system-level constraints (Etim et al., 2025). Neither study mentions weather. A null finding sitting alongside this body of caregiver-reported barriers looks less like an absence and more like confirmation that other factors are doing the explanatory work weather might otherwise be expected to do.

The second concerns a larger and more severe shock crowding out a gentler one. Vaccination access across the wider Sahel has been shown to track conflict and the breakdown of administrative infrastructure far more closely than any environmental variable, with ZD rates in conflict-affected states reaching as high as 43 per cent (Sabahelzain et al., 2025). Kano and Katsina sit within this same security environment, and a population already absorbing the effects of insecurity, displaced administrative capacity, and disrupted supply chains may simply have little remaining sensitivity to a comparatively mild stressor like a hot day or a rainy week. This is a different claim from adaptation in the physiological sense. It is a claim about which threats compete for a household's limited capacity to respond, and conflict, in this setting, plausibly wins that competition before weather is ever in contention.

The third concerns time, not presence or absence. Heat does not straightforwardly suppress outdoor activity so much as redistribute it within the day. Using anonymised cellphone location data across more than ten thousand parks in China, Zheng et al. (2023) found that hourly temperatures above 30°C and 35°C depress outdoor leisure activity by 5 and 13 per cent respectively, an effect substantially larger than daily- or monthly-resolution studies detect, because much of the apparent decline is really substitution toward cooler morning and evening hours rather than activity forgone altogether. MCHTrack's facility visits table records only a date, not a time, for every recorded visit. If caregivers in Kano and Katsina respond to a hot day by visiting a clinic earlier or later rather than not at all, this analysis has no way to detect that shift, and a true behavioural response to heat could exist entirely within a single day's data, invisible to a model that can only see whether a visit happened, not when.

The fourth concerns heat's effect on a caregiver's time and energy rather than on the act of travel itself. A longitudinal study of subsistence farmers in Burkina Faso, using wearable sensors to track physiological strain directly rather than inferring it from outcomes, found that heat stress measurably increased physical strain during labour and worsened sleep for both men and women, with farmers pacing their effort and shifting tasks to cooler hours rather than simply working through it (Eggert et al., 2025). Much of the Sahel's rural population, including caregivers in Kano and Katsina's farming communities, works outdoors for some part of most days. A hot day may not deter a clinic visit through the discomfort of travel so much as through exhaustion, reduced household labour capacity, and the resulting reshuffling of a day's priorities, a mechanism this analysis cannot separate from simple deterrence, since both would produce the same null or weak signal in a model testing only whether a visit occurred.

The fifth concerns the outcome variable itself, and is less comfortable than the first four. Siddiqi's and Samano's registries both record a clinical encounter that either happened or did not on a given day, with little reason to doubt that basic record in either case. MCHTrack's facility visits table carries the enumeration and verification problems set out across Section II. A null result against a noisier outcome cannot carry the same weight as a null result against a cleaner one, and a real weather effect, however it operates, could exist here and still be too faint for this dataset to catch.

Taken together, these five explanations point toward the same broader conclusion from a different angle each time. Weather may genuinely matter less in this setting than in Sindh or Miami, because conflict and social barriers dominate the explanatory space before weather arrives, because the data cannot see the time-shifting or labour-capacity channels through which a weather effect would most plausibly operate, or because the data itself is too noisy to detect an effect that is real but small. This thesis cannot distinguish between these explanations with the data as currently structured, a limitation returned to directly in Section V's recommendations for what MCHTrack would need to capture to test them, and the fifth explanation in particular is worth holding in mind through the next two sections, since the question of how much MCHTrack's records can be trusted on their own runs through everything that follows.

## C. The limits of ward-level analysis: what the Kano/Katsina asymmetry teaches about this kind of data more broadly

Ward-level analysis built on routine programme data tends to look most informative exactly where the underlying records are least reliable, since the same gaps that produce noisy data, incomplete enumeration, inconsistent verification, duplicate entries, can also produce the kind of extreme value a residual analysis is designed to detect. Cleaner data, by contrast, may simply show less variation, not because the underlying reality is more even, but because there is less room for error to generate an outlier. A reader working under time pressure has reason to focus on the largest numbers, even though those numbers may be the ones resting on the weakest evidence.

Section III.A.ii is a direct illustration of this general point rather than an exception to it. Katsina's ward residuals show the largest deviations from the model's predictions anywhere in this analysis. Katsina is also the state with the documented duplication problem, 38.9 per cent of facility visit records affected by a device handover, and the state where the verification gap, a tracing case closed on a card check with no record of what the card showed, has the most room to affect the underlying numbers. Kano, cleaner throughout, shows a flatter spread. The appropriate response is not a different statistical model but a verification step before any ward-level finding informs a resource decision. A flagged ward is a candidate for a field visit or a card check, not a confirmed priority, a distinction taken up directly in Section V. The same caution applies, in a different form, to the weather null just discussed: in both cases, the least reliable parts of the record are exactly where this thesis's findings are hardest to take at face value.

## D. Demand-side scope as a critical lens

This last point cuts in one direction throughout the section so far, toward where the data is too thin to confirm a finding. It is worth asking whether it also cuts the other way, toward an entire category of explanation this thesis has not been able to test at all. Section IV.B raised conflict and administrative disruption as a shock potentially severe enough to crowd out a gentler one, weather, in shaping caregiver behaviour. The same mechanism plausibly operates on the supply side, and here the evidence is more direct. Nigeria's national vaccine stock performance management dashboard, rolled out from 2014 with Gavi, Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and UNICEF support, found that gaps in stock reporting concentrated specifically in conflict-affected areas of the northeast, where basic primary healthcare delivery is itself disrupted (World Economic Forum, 2014). Separate survey work across 35 immunisation clinics in Ile-Ife, southwest Nigeria, found that only 29 per cent of vaccinators kept any record of vaccine stock-on-hand at all (Ojo et al., 2019). Weak supply-side recordkeeping, in other words, is not a unique limitation of MCHTrack. It reflects a broader pattern across Nigerian routine immunisation delivery.

This blind spot is not hypothetical, and its scale may be larger than it first appears. A Missed Opportunities for Vaccination assessment in Ondo State, using exit interviews with caregivers who had already reached a health facility, found that 32.8 per cent left without receiving an indicated vaccine, the large majority during a visit made for an unrelated reason where no one offered the vaccine, rather than a vaccination visit where the vaccine itself was unavailable on the day (Fatiregun et al., 2021). MCHTrack has no equivalent mechanism for capturing this. A facility visits row in this dataset is created only when a vaccination is actually administered, so a caregiver who reaches a clinic and leaves without one, whether through a stockout, an overlooked opportunity, or some other failure at the point of contact, leaves no trace at all. The scale of this gap cannot be estimated from MCHTrack's own records, but evidence from elsewhere in Nigeria suggests it is unlikely to be small.

This returns the discussion to the weather null in Section IV.B, this time from the supply side rather than the demand side. A flat relationship between weather and visit counts could mean caregivers are genuinely undeterred by heat or rainfall. It could equally mean that a real weather effect on caregiver attempts is being diluted by a supply-side and system-side gap of unknown but plausibly substantial size, the same gap the Ondo State exit interviews suggest exists elsewhere in the country. MCHTrack cannot distinguish a quiet day caused by low demand from a quiet day caused by caregivers arriving and being turned away. The null finding in Section IV.B should be read with this ambiguity attached, not as a clean statement that weather has no bearing on care-seeking in this setting, but as a statement that this dataset, as currently structured, cannot rule the possibility out either.

## E. Fieldwork as contextual grounding

The field material referenced throughout this chapter, conversations with DATHARM staff, two field visits to primary healthcare centres in the wider Abuja area, and internal reports shared by DATHARM, is not an independent qualitative study. No structured protocol was applied and no formal coding carried out. Its purpose is to help interpret the quantitative findings against what people working with the programme observe directly, in the manner of informal colleague commentary rather than a parallel research method, and it is where the household enumeration gap and the off-network verification gap described in Section II.A first surfaced. Treating this material as evidence, as this chapter has throughout, is defensible practice rather than a methodological shortcut: engaging directly with the people and systems generating the data under analysis is standard good practice for applied programme research, not a compromise that needs excusing.

Conversations covered DATHARM's Kano and Katsina coordinators, the data manager, and staff encountered during the two facility visits, spanning discussion of enumeration practice, tracing protocol, and day-to-day barriers caregivers are seen to face. This material is used only where it corroborates or usefully complicates a finding that already stands on its own quantitatively, not as independent confirmation in its own right, a distinction returned to directly in Section IV.F.

## F. Closing synthesis: convergence across methods

Three of this thesis's findings, distance, timing, and recordkeeping, were each corroborated by field engagement at the point each came up above. Weather's apparent irrelevance was corroborated in the same way, but by absence rather than agreement: nobody closest to the programme named it as a barrier either. None of this corroboration was gathered through a structured qualitative method, as Section IV.E made clear. It was observed informally, and is used here only where it supports a finding that already stands on its own.

**Table 4.3.  Convergence of quantitative findings and field observation**

```{r tab-4-3}
render_simple_table(show_tab("tab_4_3"), widths_em = c("22em", "20em", "10em"))
```

> Same four themes as Table 4.1, restated here to show where the regression finding and the informal field account agree (distance, timing, recordkeeping) versus where agreement is really an absence of any field mention at all (weather).

This agreement between a regression coefficient and an informal field account deserves to be taken seriously, but not overstated. It is not independent confirmation in any rigorous sense, since the field material was never collected with the structure that would require. What it offers instead is a check against a real risk of working with data like MCHTrack's: a coefficient can be statistically significant and still tell you very little true about the world, simply because the data behind it is thin in the wrong places. Where the regression and the field account agreed, that risk looks smaller. Where they did not, the largest regression deviations in Section III.A.ii sat in the state with the least reliable records, and the supply-side gap raised in Section IV.D sits entirely outside what either the regression or the field engagement could see at all. This thesis has tried to treat both kinds of disagreement, and both kinds of silence, with the same weight as the agreements, rather than setting them aside. A dissertation built on routine digital health records must state plainly where those records can be relied upon and where they cannot.

# V. Conclusion and Recommendations

## A. Implications by driver

This thesis asked what predicts ZD status and tracing effectiveness in MCHTrack. The two models answer differently, and DATHARM's two underlying problems, finding zero-dose children and getting them vaccinated once found, call for different fixes.

Distance is the strongest predictor of ZD status once the strict, no-contact-at-all definition is applied, so continued or expanded outreach into the most distant wards stands the best chance of finding children the current system is most likely to miss, an urgency sharpened by the household enumeration gap: if roughly one in five households go unreached, as DATHARM's own Kano coordinator estimates, the children furthest from a facility are plausibly also the least likely to be found at all. Distance loses almost all of its predictive power once a child is flagged and tracing begins. SMS and phone contact do the work of recovery, not physical reach, so investment in contact infrastructure is likely to do more for recovery than investment in physical reach would, though not uniformly across states, and DATHARM's existing practice of treating method choice as a local decision already reflects the right instinct.

The clearest single recommendation concerns recovery reporting itself. Recovery measured strictly sits at 42.6 per cent; measured permissively, it rises to 77.2 per cent. Neither figure is wrong, they answer different questions, and the gap between them is large enough to change how a funder or DATHARM's own leadership might judge performance. Any reported recovery figure should state which definition produced it, and where possible, both should be reported side by side. The gap was never hidden in the data; it was only ever uncollapsed.

## B. What remains unresolved about weather, and why

Section IV.B offered five explanations for the weather null: social and operational rhythm may already absorb most of the swing in daily visits before weather can register; conflict and administrative disruption may crowd out a gentler stressor entirely; a real response to heat may exist within a single day, invisible to data recorded only by date; heat may act through labour and household time rather than travel deterrence directly; and the outcome variable itself may simply be too noisy to detect an effect that is real but small.

This thesis cannot choose between these five, and the temptation to choose anyway is worth resisting on purpose. Conflict dominance is the strongest candidate by reputation, and picking it as the answer would have produced a tidier but unjustified conclusion, since nothing here rules out the other four. A structural-zero mixture model, separating the process generating zero-visit days from the count process on days something happens, was considered as a more direct test and not built given this project's timeline; it remains the clearest next modelling step, not a door closed by this thesis. Two explanations point directly to what MCHTrack would need to capture next: a time-of-day field on facility visits, and some visibility into supply-side stockouts.

## C. Limitations

Four limitations have run through this thesis. MCHTrack records children who are found, not children who exist, and the enumeration gap has no field anywhere in the system, so every ZD count inherits it silently. Katsina's facility visit records carry a documented duplication problem, worked around here but not repaired, and Katsina's reliability degrades further later in the study period, the reason the weather model uses Kano alone. Recovery can be confirmed by a card check with no record of what the card showed, producing the strict-versus-permissive gap above. This analysis also tested demand-side explanations only, with no visibility into stockouts, cold-chain failures, or staffing gaps, a blind spot evidence from elsewhere in Nigeria suggests is unlikely to be small.

A further limitation concerns what could not be measured even in principle. Household socioeconomic status, maternal education, and birth order are absent from MCHTrack's fields entirely, and the system cannot check whether a caregiver's account of a vaccination history was accurate. None of this is unique to MCHTrack. Ward-level analysis built on this kind of data tends to look most informative exactly where the records are least reliable; any system allowing a case to close on an unverified confirmation step will generate a gap between what it reports and what it can prove; a system built around demand-side identification will, by construction, be blind to supply-side failure. Organisations running similar programmes elsewhere may find these three questions worth asking of their own data. The specific numbers here belong to Kano and Katsina in this period; none of it is claimed to travel further.

## D. Future research directions

Two directions extend beyond this thesis's setting. The first is whether weather affects immunisation-seeking behaviour in this region at all, properly tested through a design built for the purpose: a longer time span letting weather vary independently of any single conflict episode or religious calendar, and fields capturing visit timing and supply-side stockouts directly. The second concerns how digital immunisation registries perform across contexts. Mantel et al. (2025) evaluated electronic immunisation registries and logistics systems across Guinea, Honduras, Rwanda, and Tanzania, documenting their methodology so it could be replicated elsewhere; no conflict-affected or Sahelian country was included. Applying the same framework to MCHTrack and comparable systems in Nigeria and the wider Sahel would test whether the limitations identified here, the enumeration gap, the verification gap, the supply-side blind spot, are general features of this kind of system or specific to this setting.

MCHTrack was built to find children the health system was missing. This thesis set out to do the same to the data itself, and to the question of weather riding alongside it. A record is not the same as the life it tries to follow. A null result is not the same as an absence. The distance between what was found and what remains unresolved is where the real work of reaching every child will always have to continue.
